claims.text: Local chemical-ordering fluctuations arise from the compositional complexity of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Local chemical-ordering fluctuations are the primary factor governing premelting and melting behavior.
Local enrichment in specific elements lowers the local energy barrier for melting.
Elementally enriched regions initiate premelting at lower temperatures than a homogeneous distribution.
A random solid solution of five or more principal elements ensures overall compositional uniformity.
The proposed comparison introduces engineered local elemental-distribution fluctuations while retaining a homogeneous random-solid-solution model as the baseline.
Local chemical enrichment induces lattice distortions.
Enrichment-induced lattice distortions act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Nonuniform local composition destabilizes the lattice.
Lattice destabilization initiates liquid-like phases in chemically enriched regions.
Heterogeneous premelting propagates through the nanoparticle at lower temperatures.
Nanoparticles with engineered compositional fluctuations will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than homogeneous nanoparticles.
Engineered compositional fluctuations will make premelting more spatially heterogeneous.
Melting initiation will be spatially correlated with elementally enriched regions.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles from 2 to 50 nm under controlled equilibrium or quasi-equilibrium simulated heating.
Under extreme nonequilibrium processing, kinetic effects may dominate premelting and melting behavior.
Simulation timescale and method resolution can limit prediction of the exact melting-temperature shift.
Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in premelting onset, or failure to observe spatial correlation with enriched regions, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described both as a statistically homogeneous random solid solution and as a perfectly homogeneous atomic distribution. A random multicomponent arrangement generally contains local statistical composition fluctuations, whereas a perfectly homogeneous atomic distribution implies their absence, so the control is not defined consistently.
